title: Database Indexing & Query Tuning: Quick Revision Notes
summary: Night-before revision of B-tree indexes, composite and covering index design, why indexes get skipped, reading EXPLAIN, writing sargable queries, and DML and constraints. Ends with a one-page cheat sheet.

chapters.title: B-tree Index Mental Model
points: Definition: a B-tree index is a sorted, balanced tree of key values pointing to rows; a key lookup is O(log n), and a range scan or ORDER BY on the key is O(log n + k) for the k rows read
Mechanism: root → internal nodes → leaf pages; leaves are linked in key order, so a range scan finds the start once and then walks the leaves
Comparison: index seek (jump to a key, few reads) vs full table scan (read every row); an index wins when the query touches a small fraction of rows
Example: CREATE INDEX idx_orders_cust ON orders(customer_id); then WHERE customer_id = 42 seeks the tree instead of scanning the table
Mistake: indexing every column; each index costs disk space and slows INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE, and low-selectivity columns (gender, boolean) rarely help

chapters.title: Composite and Covering Indexes
points: Definition: a composite index on (a, b, c) is sorted by a, then b within a, then c within b
Leftmost-prefix rule: (a,b,c) serves filters on a, a+b and a+b+c, but not b alone or c alone
Column order: put equality columns first, the range column last, and break ties by higher selectivity; columns after a range condition cannot narrow the seek

Covering index: if every column the query needs is in the index, the engine answers from the index alone (Index Only Scan / 'Using index') with no table lookup; add extra columns with INCLUDE (Postgres, SQL Server) or as trailing key columns (MySQL)
Mistake: creating (a) and (a,b) both; the composite already serves queries on a, so the single-column index is redundant

chapters.title: When Indexes Are Not Used
points: Function or expression on the column defeats the index: WHERE YEAR(created_at) = 2025 or WHERE LOWER(email) = 'a@b.com' (fix: rewrite the predicate, or build a functional index)
Leading wildcard: LIKE '%abc' cannot use the B-tree, but LIKE 'abc%' can because it is a range on the prefix
Implicit type conversion: comparing a VARCHAR column to a number (WHERE phone = 5551234) forces a cast on every row and skips the index
Low selectivity or tiny table: the optimizer picks a full scan when the query returns a large share of rows (often more than roughly 10-20%) because random lookups would cost more
Other skips: OR across different columns, <> / NOT IN, a violated leftmost prefix, and stale statistics (run ANALYZE / UPDATE STATISTICS)

chapters.title: EXPLAIN and Sargable Queries
points: Definition: EXPLAIN shows the planned execution without running the query; EXPLAIN ANALYZE (Postgres, MySQL 8) runs it and adds actual times and row counts
Read the plan for: access type (Seq Scan / type=ALL means full scan, vs Index Scan / Index Seek / ref / range), the chosen key, estimated rows, and join order
Red flags: Seq Scan on a large table, estimated rows far from actual rows (stale stats), a Sort node or 'Using filesort' that a better index could remove
Sargable means the predicate can seek an index: keep the bare column on one side, so WHERE created_at >= '2025-01-01' AND created_at < '2026-01-01' beats WHERE YEAR(created_at) = 2025
Sargable rewrites: amount + 10 > 100 → amount > 90; LIKE '%x' → prefix search or full-text index; varchar_col = 5 on a VARCHAR column → varchar_col = '5'; avoid SELECT * so covering indexes can apply

chapters.title: DML and Constraints
points: DML statements: INSERT INTO t(cols) VALUES (...), UPDATE t SET c = v WHERE ..., DELETE FROM t WHERE ...; always run UPDATE and DELETE inside a transaction and with a WHERE clause
Indexing cost of DML: every INSERT or DELETE touches all indexes on the table, and an UPDATE touches every index that contains a changed column, so write-heavy tables should keep few indexes
PRIMARY KEY = NOT NULL + UNIQUE, one per table, and creates a clustered or unique index; UNIQUE allows NULLs (count varies by engine) and also creates an index

FOREIGN KEY enforces referential integrity with ON DELETE CASCADE / SET NULL / RESTRICT; the engine does not auto-index the child column in Postgres or SQL Server, so index FK columns yourself to speed joins and parent deletes

DELETE removes rows one by one and is logged and rollback-able; TRUNCATE empties the table fast and resets identity in MySQL and SQL Server (PostgreSQL only with TRUNCATE ... RESTART IDENTITY); CHECK and NOT NULL guard values, and DEFAULT fills omitted columns

chapters.title: Indexing and Query Tuning Cheat Sheet
points: Index design rule: equality columns, then ORDER BY columns, then the range column last (equality then range only optimises the seek; ORDER BY columns after a range column cannot remove the sort); remember the leftmost prefix
Index not used if: function on column, leading %, type mismatch, low selectivity, OR across columns, stale stats
Tuning loop: run EXPLAIN ANALYZE → spot Seq Scan, filesort or bad estimates → add or reorder an index or rewrite the predicate → re-run EXPLAIN and compare
Covering index check: plan shows Index Only Scan or 'Using index' → no table lookup
Constraints: PK = NOT NULL + UNIQUE; FK needs a manual index in Postgres; DELETE is logged and filtered, TRUNCATE is fast and unfiltered
